vignette:
Mrs. Tran speaks of her life in two distinct parts: before the helicopters and after. She is eighty now, a respected elder who teaches Buddhist principles to children at the local temple. Her hands, when she pours tea, are steady. Her voice, when she chants, is clear. But in the quiet of our sessions, she unravels the sixty years of silence she has kept since she was a young woman named Lien.

The first part of her life ended in April of 1975. She describes the heat, the suffocating press of the crowd outside the embassy walls in Saigon. The air was thick with the smells of diesel, sweat, and a metallic, coppery fear. She and her new husband, Hieu, were just two faces in a sea of thousands, their hands locked together so tightly that the bones ached. The defining sound of those days was the rhythmic *whump-whump-whump* of the American helicopters. It was the sound of a closing door, a sound that promised both salvation and damnation.

She doesn't remember the flight itself, only the terror of the final scramble over the wall. She remembers losing a sandal and feeling the hot asphalt burn the sole of her foot. She remembers the look on the face of a woman who didn't make it on, a face she still sees superimposed over the cashiers at the grocery store. Hieu was pragmatic, focused. He pulled her forward, his grip like iron. He was already living in the "after." Lien was still there, one foot bare on the burning ground.

They made a life in America. Two children, a small but successful fabric store, and eventually, grandchildren whose uncomplicated laughter feels like a broadcast from a foreign planet. For decades, the past was a box she kept locked and buried. Hieu never wanted to talk about it. “We are here now,” he would say, a gentle but firm period at the end of any potential sentence about their escape. She followed his lead, channeling her energy into her family, her business, and eventually, her work at the temple. She taught children about mindfulness, about letting go of attachment to suffering. She spoke the words, and a part of her even believed them.

But the body keeps the score. For sixty years, she has slept no more than three hours a night. She startles violently if Hieu touches her shoulder from behind. The sound of a lawnmower starting unexpectedly, or a low-flying news helicopter, can send a jolt of pure adrenaline through her, leaving her hands trembling and her heart pounding in her ears. She arranges the furniture in every room so that she can always see the door. Her family sees these things as quirks, the eccentricities of an old woman.

Recently, it has become worse. It was the Fourth of July last year. The neighborhood fireworks began, and the percussive thumps sent her diving to the floor, her hands over her head. She was no longer in her manicured suburban backyard; she was back in the suffocating heat of Saigon, the explosions rattling her bones. Hieu tried to comfort her, but his touch felt alien. She couldn't stop shaking for hours.

Now, even the temple, her sanctuary, feels unsafe. The scent of burning incense, meant to be calming, catches in her throat and reminds her of the smoke that choked the city. While guiding children through a meditation on loving-kindness, her mind will betray her, flashing on the image of that woman’s face at the embassy wall. She feels like a fraud, teaching a peace she has never known. She tells me she is a ghost, haunting a life that someone else was supposed to live.
